title: How to Build Systems That Survive Hard Days
author: Ben Meer
summary: This guest post on Nir Eyal's newsletter, adapted from Ben Meer's book How to Be Good at Life, argues that a well-timeboxed plan still fails unless it is built to bend. Meer opens with the Ever Given stuck in the Suez Canal as an image of an optimized system with no slack. He offers the Four B's as a framework for resilience: buffers, barriers, backups and beacons. Buffers add time or capacity to absorb surprises, barriers make predictable failures harder, backups define a smaller Plan B using if-then implementation intentions, and beacons are early-warning signals that tell you when to shift into maintenance mode. The practical advice is concrete, such as fifteen minutes between meetings, removing the remote's batteries, and pre-dating the holiday window. He ends by asking the reader to look at next week and ask where the plan is most likely to break.
points: Efficiency pushed too far becomes fragility, so a schedule built for perfect conditions will cascade into failure at the first delay.
Buffers such as gaps between meetings and a daily pressure-release block give surprises somewhere to go instead of derailing the next commitment.
Barriers work by changing the environment so the right choice is made less often in the moment, for example by adding friction to mindless habits.
Backups use implementation intentions to pre-decide a smaller Plan B, which prevents the all-or-nothing collapse after one disruption.
Beacons and a dated maintenance mode let you lower the bar deliberately during predictable stress periods rather than quitting the system.
quotes: A single stuck vessel exposed how vulnerable a tightly optimized system can become when there is no room for anything to go wrong.

In our own lives, it can be tempting to chase efficiency over resilience. We build schedules for perfect conditions, assuming every meeting ends on time, our energy holds, traffic cooperates, and nothing unexpected happens.
Buffers are cushions of extra time, money, or capacity that absorb surprises.
Good barriers reduce how often you have to make the right choice in the moment.
Here’s where I used to go wrong: I would treat one disruption like failure and abandon the system entirely. But that all-or-nothing mindset often leads to nothing at all.
But they are just as useful for building Plan B: If work blows up my 6 p.m. workout, then I will do a 10-minute bodyweight workout at home.
Beacons are early-warning signals that help you spot trouble before it becomes a crisis.
The Ever Given exposed the danger of efficiency without resilience. Push efficiency too far, and it becomes fragility.
